svg.title: Antiepileptic mechanisms and seizure-type spectrum
svg.desc: Four mechanism rows: sodium-channel blockade (phenytoin, carbamazepine, lamotrigine, lacosamide) for partial and tonic-clonic seizures; T-type calcium blockade (ethosuximide) for absence; GABA enhancement (benzodiazepines, phenobarbital, vigabatrin, tiagabine); broad agents (valproate, levetiracetam, topiramate). Status epilepticus ladder: lorazepam IV, then fosphenytoin, levetiracetam or valproate, then midazolam or propofol anaesthesia.
svg.text: Match the channel to the seizure type; status runs a fixed time ladder
Phenytoin (zero-order kinetics, gingival hyperplasia, HLA-B*1502 risk) - carbamazepine (autoinduction, SIADH) -
lamotrigine (Stevens-Johnson rash) - lacosamide (PR prolongation). Use: partial + tonic-clonic, never absence.
Ethosuximide: absence seizures with 3 Hz spike-wave (hyperventilation provokes). First line for pure absence.
Benzodiazepines + phenobarbital (open Cl- channel) - vigabatrin (irreversible GABA transaminase block, visual field
loss) - tiagabine (blocks GABA reuptake). Sedation and tolerance limit chronic use.
Na+ blockers worsen absence and myoclonic epilepsy: never give phenytoin or carbamazepine for absence.
Absence starts young (ethosuximide); myoclonic needs valproate or levetiracetam; status over 5 minutes is time-is-brain.
Phenytoin needs level monitoring (free fraction rises in hypoalbuminaemia); carbamazepine autoinduces its own metabolism.
